sentence: We will show that if a₁, a₂, …, aₙ is any monotone (say increasing) sequence of n distinct real numbers, then the number of 3‐term arithmetic progressions that can occur (that is, triples 1 ≤ i < j < k ≤ n with
2·aⱼ = aᵢ + aₖ

)
cannot exceed
In particular, if we write n = 2m for even n and n = 2m + 1 for odd n, then the maximum number is
One may check that these formulas are equivalent to the answer given in binomial coefficient notation.
Below we explain why this number is the best possible and show that it is attained by an arithmetic progression.

────────────────────────────
Understanding the Structure
Suppose a₁, a₂, …, aₙ is increasing.
A 3‐term arithmetic progression (AP) is a triple of indices (i, j, k), with i < j < k, such that
aⱼ – aᵢ = aₖ – aⱼ   or, equivalently,  2·aⱼ = aᵢ + aₖ.
Notice that if we have an arithmetic progression in the usual sense then the three terms are “evenly spaced” (in the number line).
One natural candidate for maximizing the number of these AP’s is to choose the sequence itself to be an arithmetic progression.
(It turns out that no other choice can produce more 3‐AP’s.

────────────────────────────
The Case When the Sequence is an Arithmetic Progression

Assume
  a₁, a₂, …, aₙ  with  aᵢ = A + (i – 1)d    (with d ≠ 0)
for some constant A.

Then for any indices i < j < k we have:
  aᵢ = A + (i – 1)d,
  aⱼ = A + (j – 1)d,
  aₖ = A + (k – 1)d.

The condition for (aᵢ, aⱼ, aₖ) to be an arithmetic progression is
  2·[A + (j – 1)d] = [A + (i – 1)d] + [A + (k – 1)d].

Working out the algebra,
  2A + 2(j – 1)d = 2A + (i + k – 2)d,
so we must have
  2(j – 1) = (i + k – 2)
    or  2j = i + k.
Thus, in an arithmetic progression, a triple (i, j, k) forms an AP if and only if j is exactly the average of i and k, which means that i + k must be even and then j = (i + k)/2.

────────────────────────────
Counting the Number of AP’s
Once the sequence is chosen to be arithmetic, every pair of indices (i,k) with i < k and i + k even produces exactly one AP (namely, with j = (i + k)/2).
Thus, the number of 3‐term AP’s is exactly the number of pairs (i, k) with 1 ≤ i < k ≤ n such that i + k is even.
Now, when is the sum i + k even?
Recall that the sum of two integers is even if and only if both integers have the same parity (both even or both odd).
In the set {1, 2, …, n}: • The number of odd numbers is ⌈n/2⌉.
• The number of even numbers is ⌊n/2⌋.
Therefore, the number of pairs (i, k) with both indices odd is C(⌈n/2⌉, 2) and the number with both even is C(⌊n/2⌋, 2).
Hence, the total number of AP’s is
Let’s write these numbers more explicitly.

────────────────────────────
Writing the Answer Explicitly
Case 1.
n is even.
Write n = 2m.
• Then, the number of odd indices = m and even indices = m.

• Thus, the number of 3‐AP’s is
  C(m,2) + C(m,2) = (m(m – 1)/2) + (m(m – 1)/2) = m(m – 1).
Case 2.
n is odd.
Write n = 2m + 1.
• Then, the number of odd indices = m + 1 and even indices = m.

• Thus, the number of 3‐AP’s is
  C(m + 1, 2) + C(m, 2)
    = [m(m + 1)/2] + [m(m – 1)/2]
    = [m² + m + m² – m] / 2
    = (2m²)/2 = m².

So, summarizing, the maximum number of 3‐term arithmetic progressions possible in a monotone sequence (of n distinct reals) is:
  • m(m – 1) if n = 2m (even),
  • m²    if n = 2m + 1 (odd).

Or equivalently, one may simply write:
  Maximum number = C(⌈n/2⌉,2) + C(⌊n/2⌋,2).

────────────────────────────
Why This is the Maximum
One might wonder if there is another way to assign n distinct reals in increasing order such that there are more 3‐term arithmetic progressions than in the arithmetic progression case.
The key observation is that for any increasing sequence, if a triple (aᵢ, aⱼ, aₖ) is to form a three‐term AP, then the indices i, j, and k must satisfy 2aⱼ = aᵢ + aₖ.
In an arithmetic progression the relation 2aⱼ = aᵢ + aₖ is “automatically” forced by the equal spacing.
In a non‐arithmetic progression, there is less “structure” and the chance that 2aⱼ equals aᵢ + aₖ for any given three indices is even smaller.
In fact, one can show that the arithmetic progression maximizes the number of solutions to 2aⱼ = aᵢ + aₖ.
Thus, the maximum possible number of three‐term arithmetic progressions in a monotone sequence of n distinct reals is

which can also be written as:
  • m(m – 1) if n = 2m,
  • m²    if n = 2m + 1.
This is the answer.
